title: Opposite pointers
sub: Two Sum II, Container With Most Water, 3Sum — and the proof that a move loses nothing
cards/0/body:
Two Sum II (LeetCode #167). The array numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order; find two numbers that add up to target and return their indices starting from one. There is exactly one answer, 2 ≤ n ≤ 3·10⁴, and extra memory must be O(1).

The dictionary from Two Sum would solve it in O(n) but take O(n) memory — the problem forbids that. Signals of opposite pointers:

1. The array is sorted — or can be sorted, because the original indices are not needed.
2. You look for a pair by a quantity that the two ends move in opposite directions: moving the left end right increases the sum, moving the right end left decreases it. Then the sign of the error tells you which one to move.
3. Memory must be O(1).

lo and hi start at the ends. Sum too small — lo++, too large — hi--. Each step shrinks the range by one, so there are at most n − 1 steps. You already saw the same opposite pointers in Valid Palindrome — there they just compared characters.
cards/1/q: Where do opposite pointers work? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: How many pairs in a sorted array have a sum less than target
cards/1/options/1: Does a sorted array contain two numbers whose difference is exactly k
cards/1/options/2: Does a string read the same in both directions
cards/1/options/3: The pair whose sum is closest to target in an unsorted array — you need the numbers, not the indices
cards/1/options/4: A pair with sum target in an unsorted array — you need the original indices
cards/1/explain: Pairs with a sum below target: the two ends move the sum in opposite directions (how exactly to count comes at the end of the lesson). A palindrome uses the opposite pointers from the previous lesson. Closest sum: indices are not needed — sort and walk from the ends. The difference is the trap: moving either end inward decreases it, the moves have no opposite effect, and the sign of the error does not tell you which one to move; two pointers in the same direction work there. Original indices are lost by sorting — that is the dictionary.
cards/2/body:
The interviewer’s key question: “What if the answer is a pair with the lo you just discarded?” Let us prove it by elimination.

Picture all pairs (i, j), i < j, as the upper triangle of a table. Suppose numbers[lo] + numbers[hi] < target. For any j ≤ hi: numbers[j] ≤ numbers[hi], so numbers[lo] + numbers[j] < target. None of the remaining pairs with numbers[lo] works — the whole row lo is discarded, and lo++ is safe. Symmetrically, if the sum is too large, numbers[hi] is too large even with the smallest remaining number — we discard the column hi.

Invariant: if an answer exists, it is a pair inside [lo, hi]. Each step discards a whole row or column, n − 1 pairs are checked instead of n(n − 1)/2 — and none that matters is lost.

The template “say we move this end; every pair with it is worse or impossible” proves the other problems of this lesson too.
cards/3/q: numbers = [2, 3, 5, 8, 11], target = 16. lo is on 2, hi is on 11: the sum 13 is less than 16. Why does lo++ lose nothing?
cards/3/options/0: Every remaining pair with 2 is at most 2 + 11 = 13 — none of them reaches 16
cards/3/options/1: 2 is the smallest number, and the smallest numbers are never in the answer
cards/3/options/2: The pointers must move in turns, otherwise they never meet
cards/3/explain: The largest partner of 2 is 11, and even with it the sum is 13 < 16. So the whole row “2 + anything” has no answer. The answer here is 5 + 11: lo will reach the 5, and hi stays on 11.
cards/3/wrong/1: A small number can well be in the answer: with target = 5 the answer is 2 + 3. We drop 2 not because it is small, but because no remaining pair with it works.
cards/3/wrong/2: There are no turns: we move the end that is proven exhausted. The pointers meet anyway — every step shrinks the range.
cards/4/title: Container With Most Water: move the shorter line
cards/4/body:
Container With Most Water (#11). The array h holds the heights of vertical lines at positions 0..n − 1. Two lines and the axis form a container holding min(h[l], h[r]) · (r − l) water. Find the maximum. n ≤ 10⁵, h ≤ 10⁴ — the area is at most 10⁹, an int is enough.

Checking all pairs is O(n²), 5·10⁹ for n = 10⁵. Opposite pointers: start with the widest pair and move the shorter line.

Proof by elimination. Suppose h[l] < h[r]. All remaining pairs with l are (l, k), k < r: narrower, and their height min(h[l], h[k]) ≤ h[l]. None is better than the current one — line l is exhausted, l++. Moving the taller one is pointless: h[l] still limits the height while the width drops. With equal heights both are exhausted — either can move.

This is not a game problem, but it is exactly where interviewers check the proof: “how do you know you did not skip the best pair?”.
cards/5/explain: The shorter line holds the water — Math.Min. The width is the distance between the lines, r − l, not the number of positions. Move the shorter one: if the left is lower, l++. With h[l] > h[r] the code would move the taller line and skip better pairs.
cards/6/task: Step through the trace on [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]. The rig stops twice: name the area and which pointer the code moves.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: L = 1 (height 8), R = 8 (height 7). What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: min(8, 7) · (8 − 1) = 49 — a new record. The right line is lower: every remaining pair with it is narrower and no higher than 7, so it is exhausted — r--. 56 = 8 · 7 would use the taller line’s height, but the shorter one holds the water.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: L = 1 (height 8), R = 6 (height 8): equal heights. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: min(8, 8) · (6 − 1) = 40, the record 49 stays. With equal heights both lines are exhausted: any remaining pair with either of them is narrower and cannot get higher than 8. The code moves R because the condition h[l] < h[r] is strict and goes to else on a tie.
cards/7/title: 3Sum: sort, fix one element, skip duplicates
cards/7/body:
3Sum (#15). Find all unique triples [a, b, c] from the array that sum to 0. 3 ≤ n ≤ 3000. Checking all triples is n³/6 ≈ 4.5·10⁹ — far too many.

Reduce it to Two Sum II: sort (O(n log n)), fix nums[i] and use opposite pointers on [i + 1, n − 1] to find a pair summing to −nums[i]. Each i costs O(n), O(n²) in total: 9·10⁶ for n = 3000.

Duplicates. Triples are unique by value. If nums[i] == nums[i − 1], skip i: all triples with that first number are already found — the previous i had the whole range to its right, including this element. After a hit, move l and r past equal values. Compare with the previous element: the check nums[i] == nums[i + 1] skips the first of the equal ones — and with it triples like [−1, −1, 2], where it needs its twin as a partner.

A dictionary instead of pointers is also O(n²), but removing duplicates with it hurts more — you need a HashSet of triples. A small speed-up: if nums[i] > 0, only positives remain — you can stop.
cards/8/task: Step through the trace on [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]. The rig asks twice what the code does: watch i, L and R and where duplicates are skipped.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: The sum is too small — L++
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: We fixed −1 (i = 1). L = 2 points to another −1, R = 5 to 2. What happens next?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: −1 + (−1) + 2 = 0 — a triple. Skipping duplicates applies only to i: the same value in the first-number slot. Here the second −1 sits in the pair — that is a different triple, and it must not be lost.
cards/8/goal/asks/1/q: After two hits i = 2, and it is −1 again. What does the code do?
cards/8/goal/asks/1/explain: All triples with −1 as the first number were found at i = 1: it had the whole range to its right, including the second −1. So i = 2 is skipped — otherwise [-1, 0, 1] would come out twice.
cards/9/q: On [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4] this code returns only [[-1, 0, 1]]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/9/explain: After sorting: [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]. At i = 1 the code sees that nums[2] is also −1 and skips — but only the first −1 has the second −1 in its range, which [-1, -1, 2] needs. Compare with the previous one: i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i − 1] skips a repeat after the first of the equal ones has done its work.
cards/10/title: Variations: k-Sum, closest sum, counting pairs
cards/10/body:
3Sum Closest (#16): the same scheme, but instead of “found” you keep the sum closest to target. O(n²).

4Sum (#18): two nested fixed indices plus opposite pointers — O(n³). In general, k-Sum is k − 2 nested loops with opposite pointers inside: O(nk−1). In 4Sum the numbers go up to 10⁹, and a sum of four overflows an int (maximum 2,147,483,647) — add in long.

How many pairs sum to less than target (sorted array): if a[lo] + a[hi] < target, then a[lo] works with every number to its right up to hi — that is hi − lo pairs at once, then lo++. Elimination here counts pairs by whole rows. With sorting, O(n log n).

Indices needed, array unsorted — sorting loses them: either a dictionary (O(n) memory) or sort an array of indices by value.
cards/10/deep:
Proof for counting. If a[lo] + a[hi] < target, then a[lo] + a[j] ≤ a[lo] + a[hi] for every j ≤ hi — all hi − lo pairs of the row qualify, and the row is closed. If the sum is ≥ target, column hi gives no pair with any remaining lo, and it is closed. Every pair is counted exactly once.

Sorting in .NET. Array.Sort is introsort: quicksort, switching to heapsort when recursion gets too deep and to insertion sort on short ranges. Worst case O(n log n), in place, O(log n) stack, not stable — irrelevant for plain numbers. Span<T>.Sort appeared in .NET 5; Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) does not have it — sort an array, or a NativeArray<T> via Sort() from com.unity.collections.

Faster than O(n²) for 3Sum. No algorithm noticeably faster than quadratic is known: the best ones only shave logarithmic factors. The bound is so well known that hardness proofs for other problems are built on it. In an interview, O(n²) is the optimal answer.

Allocations in 3Sum. Every triple is a new int[3], plus the List growing. On a hot path in a game you would return a flat buffer of triples or write into the caller’s Span, not a list of arrays.
cards/11/q: 4Sum via “sort + two fixed indices + opposite pointers”, numbers up to 10⁹ in absolute value. What is true?
cards/11/options/0: O(n³) time, add the four numbers in long
cards/11/options/1: O(n²) time, add the four numbers in long
cards/11/options/2: O(n³) time, int is enough: four numbers up to 10⁹ sum to less than 4·10⁹
cards/11/explain: Two nested fixed indices give n² combinations, and each one runs an O(n) opposite-pointer pass: O(n³) in total, i.e. k-Sum with k = 4 is O(n^(k−1)). A sum up to 4·10⁹ does not fit in an int, whose maximum is about 2.1·10⁹.
cards/11/wrong/1: The two fixed indices alone give n² pairs, and there is an O(n) pass inside.
cards/11/wrong/2: int.MaxValue = 2,147,483,647 ≈ 2.1·10⁹ — a sum up to 4·10⁹ overflows.
cards/12/q: You are solving Container With Most Water out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: n, the range of heights, whether you need the area or the lines themselves
cards/12/items/1: Brute force over pairs: O(n²), 5·10⁹ for n = 10⁵
cards/12/items/2: Idea: start with the widest pair and move the shorter line
cards/12/items/3: Prove it: every remaining pair with the shorter line is narrower and no higher — it is exhausted
cards/12/items/4: Code while narrating: best = max(best, min · width)
cards/12/items/6: Complexity O(n), memory O(1); edge cases: two lines, equal heights
cards/12/explain: The proof comes before the code: on this problem it is exactly what the interviewer waits for. The example with two 8s also checks equal heights.
